PROPOSED TAPS TANKER ROUTE-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43 I ask leave to move a motion on a matter of major significance and timeliness. It is prompted by the failure of the government to convey to the United States government its views on the TAPS oil tanker route. In order that the interests of the people of Canada may find expression, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin):
That this House formally oppose the TAPS oil tanker route proposal as an unwarranted and unacceptable threat to the ecological rights and economic interests of Canada; and this House instructs the Secretary of State for External Affairs to transmit the above resolution to the Secretary of State of the United States of America, and since the protection of ecological heritage is increasingly the concern of the international community, that a copy be also transmitted to the Secretary General of the United Nations.

April 2, 1971

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: EAST PAKISTAN-INFORMATION ON ALLEGED BLOODSHED AND GENOCIDE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, unfortunately we have no direct communications which would enable us to decide the extent of the bloodshed going on in East Pakistan. We are very deeply concerned. speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
The House resumed, from Thursday, April 1, consideration in committee of Bill C-207, respecting the organization of the Government of Canada and matters related or incidental thereto-Mr. Trudeau-Mr. Honey in the chair.
One clause 14-Establishment of Ministries of State.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Order, please. When the committee rose yesterday clause 14 of the bill was being considered.
Yesterday the hon. member for Lotbiniere moved, with the consent of the Committee, an amendment to clause 14. Hon. members will recall that the Chair took under advisement the procedural acceptability of the amendment. If I may, I would now rule on the matter. Perhaps first I should read the amendment:
That clause 14 of the Act respecting the organization of the Government of Canada and matters related or incidental thereto, be amended by deleting lines 23 to 25 and substituting therefor the following:
"Parliament may pass an Act amending the Act respecting the organization of the Government of Canada and having the effect of creating a Ministry of State."
Last evening I indicated I had some doubt concerning the procedural acceptability of the amendment. I indicated, however, I would like to think about it and would be prepared to hear today any hon. gentlemen who might wish to argue the procedural acceptability of the amendment. I might say that in the intervening time I have confirmed my preliminary thought that the motion is not procedurally acceptable on two points. First, it is declaratory, and as such I do not think comes within the purview of the clause we are presently considering. The second point, which I also think is important, is that as all hon. members know, Parliament is its own master and may enact legislation or statutes as it wishes within the confines of its constitutional authority. In effect, the amendment of the hon. member for Lotbiniere confirms this. I believe the amendment is a nullity in the sense that it is not necessary to say what is obvious, and the
[Mr. Speaker.!
obvious of course is that Parliament may legislate at any time to do the things it wishes to do within its constitutional authority. These are the points which would seem to indicate the amendment is out of order. However, if hon. members wish to present argument I would be pleased to hear it.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have listened with great interest to your first remarks concerning the admissibility of the amendment I submitted yesterday with regard to clause 14 of Bill C-207. You question the merits of the amendment, and for the most part you base your decision on two points.
First, you say that this may be more in the nature of a statement than of an amendment. You add that there is no need to speak of the power of Parliament as this power is evident.
I would like to comment on your second point first. There is no evidence, at the present time, that Parliament is its own master, with regard to clause 14. It is neither certain, nor clearly indicated that Parliament will be able to appoint ministers through the agency of government, or to participate in a debate on the establishment of new ministries.
Mr. Chairman, it is obvious, and I agree it is, that when the government wants to set up a Crown corporation, a ministry of state or a federal department-and there are numerous precedents to enlighten us in this regard-it is clear that Parliament has its word to say about it and that it must pass legislation, that is to say, the government's desire to establish a particular department must be approved by Parliament.
But the procedure proposed in clause 14 is an exceptional one which does not give Parliament this authority to legislate on the establishment of a ministry of state. This is, indeed, what can be read in clause 14, and I quote:
[DOT]-the Governor in Council may, by proclamation, establish a Ministry of State for that purpose.
Nothing is said about Parliament, and I will point out that this is a truly exceptional procedure as regards the setting up of a ministry.
It is precisely this concern which prompted me to move an amendment which is not a substantive one, and there is the second point of my argument.
Indeed, one can conclude from the heading of this clause that the substance of the matter is the establishment of ministries of state. Essentially, the question is therefore to know if we are in favour of the establishment of ministries of state or against it, and I will point out that my amendment does not aim at changing the substance of the matter directly or indirectly. The amendment that I have moved deals only with form and procedure, and I am not against the establishment of ministries of state, because I would then change the substance of the matter. In the 4th edition of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, it is clearly stated that the substance of the matter cannot be altered, but that the form and procedure can be.
April 2, 1971

The government proposes in clause 14 the terms "Governor in Council" instead of "Parliament" and "proclamation" instead of "legislation."
Mr. Chairman, I will respectfully point out that even if I agree with you that it is not necessary-because obviously Parliament is supreme-to refer to the powers of Parliament, if we do not wish to use the terms "Governor in Council" or "proclamation", it is necessary to make things clear to state who will have the authority, if we do not agree about the procedure.
This is why althoug it seems obvious to us members that Parliament is the supreme authority, it is not evident from clause 14 because this clause denies Parliament this supreme power to legislate on the establishment of ministries of state, of departments and of Crown corporations.
Mr. Chairman, the amendment that I moved precisely opposed this procedure.
Then, Mr. Chairman, you give a general indication saying that we are free to make recommendations and give advice, which we appreciate respectfully.
You say that the amendment would appear to be a statement of some sort.
noon)
In fact, this is not a statement but a simple change in procedure with respect to the creation of ministries of state.
Here is a part of the amendment:
Parliament may pass an Act amending the Act respecting the organization of the Government of Canada and having the effect of creating a Ministry of State.
During the debate yesterday the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis) told the House the amendment was out of order because it anticipates the intentions of the government.
I refer the House to Hansard of which everyone has a copy.
Mr. Chairman, if the argument of the hon. member for Ottawa West were right, we should logically say the same thing about this clause.
Indeed one can read this in the bill:
-the Governor in Council may, by proclamation, establish a Ministry of State for that purpose.
This clause therefore presupposes the intentions of the government and legislates, without giving Parliament any justification, on the necessity of creating ministries of state.
In other words, if my amendment has no bearing on an immediate and concrete reality, neither does clause 14: it relates to the possibility that some day the government might want to establish a ministry of state. In short, one is no better than the other.
Mr. Chairman, if the argument of the hon. member for Ottawa West seems in order to you, I respectfully submit that the same goes for my amendment; they both amount to the same thing.

The clause stipulates that the "Governor in Council may"; in the amendment, you can read: "the Parliament may". These are the same circumstances. The only change, Mr. Chairman, is in the procedure, the manner, the means, and not in the substance, the principle.
The principle is clearly indicated in the heading:
Ministries of State for Specified Purposes.
Mr. Chairman, thus this is not a future statement, since clause 14, at that rate, could also be a future statement, as the clause stipulates: "the Governor in Council may". As a matter of fact, what is clause 14 but a statement? It says:
Where it appears to the Governor in Council that the requirements for formulating and developing new and comprehensive policies in relation to any matter or matters-
Mr. Chairman, these are such general terms that they are merely a statement of intent. Clause 14 is a statement of intent, some sort of a blank cheque to the government which one day or another, depending upon requirements, will establish a "ministry of state".
It is not mentioned whether this is a specific legislation. The names of the ministries are not mentioned and it is not said how many there will be. It is not specified in which fields they will work, study, formulate or develop their programs. The bill merely states that there will be "ministries of state" according to the "requirements for formulating and developing new and comprehensive policies"; all it says is that there will be ministries in relation to any matter or matters. It does not legislate in any specific field.
For this reason, Mr. Chairman, I suggest that if it can be said that my amendment is declaratory, clause 14 is also declaratory on the same ground. And if it can be legislated truly on a statement, granting that clause 14 is a statement of fact, since it really is, why should we not have the right to legislate at the same level?
This is not a question of money, but of legislating at the same level. For these reasons-and I apologize for taking so much of the time of the House to explain and defend the amendment which I proposed-it seems to me that the amendment does not deal with substance but with procedure, and that this is an excellent opportunity for the government, if it is willing to accept the amendment, to prove that it considers the substance, namely, the creation of "ministries of state"-if it is really necessary-more important than the ways, the means, the procedure to achieve it. If the government feels that the substance is more important than the form, then why should they not make concessions about the form, about the means of reaching the same end, that is the setting up of "ministries of state", of passing legislation in areas relating to "new and comprehensive policies".

The hon. member will have to do better. As I was saying, criticism of the bill goes far beyond the pork barrel aspect. The part of the bill we are now considering would allow the government to set up, and then dismantle, a whole series of departments without any parliamentary approval. This is what was worrying the hon. member for Lotbiniere.
The pitfalls are obvious. This is another step in the degradation of Parliament. I do not pretend that Parliament is the totality of democracy in Canada, but in this country it is certainly one of the most vital and basic links in the democratic chain. Any attempt to whittle down its rights is an attack on the democratic process, and that this is the effect of this bill has surely been adequately demonstrated already. Why then is there this determination on the part of the government?
The hon. member for Lotbiniere said on Wednesday that the setting up of these new structures now is simply a means of trying to hide inefficiency. I certainly go along with that analysis. The government knows, or ought to know by this time what the basic problems are, but it seems to be attempting to give itself a sort of panel of panic buttons to press when it is faced with some kind of unexpected event. In other words, we have another instance of government by ad hoc measures; this time we might call it institutionalized ad hocism. After three years in power, government is still looking at machinery instead of dealing with issues, and still dealing with structures instead of concrete reforms. This clearly became a government by way of improvisation. Look at the action with regard to Denison, just off the top of the head. Look at the action with regard to Home Oil, just off the top of the head. It was not part of any policy. Yet this government, Mr. Chairman, is supposed to be a program government, a government that knew what it was doing. This doesn't say much for its over-all competence or its ability to forecast.
Once again, as in so many spheres, we are faced with ambiguity and uncertainty. This time, the government intends to institutionalize these two characteristics by process of law. It must be the first time that a democratic government has openly admitted its own

Government Organization Act, 1970 incompetence and lack of foresight. We have had enough experience with improvising, Mr. Chairman, to deepen our concern that a provision such as we are now considering would increase the certainty of ambiguity and the certainty of confusion.
Three sources of deep concern about this measure relate to the integrity of Parliament. This measure represents an attack on the essential dignity of the Member of Parliament. I realize there is a problem in this age of growing executive power, but the solution of this government for the great majority of government Members of Parliament, is to try to include them in the charmed circle of executive perquisites. In other words, the sweets of office are handed around to everyone.
We have another dimension to the extent of confusion now, Mr. Chairman, the confusion that exists among ministers and parliamentary assistants. The ordinary Member of Parliament is usually considered to be expressing his own views unless he is explicitly expressing government views. Until the era of this government it was assumed that ministers expressed government policy when they spoke, but not now. It all commenced with the debate on NATO in which the Minister of Communications expressed totally different views from those of the Ministers of External Affairs and National Defence who had some responsibility.
More recently there has been the matter of Alaskan Oil. We have the Secretary of State for External Affairs expressing disapproval of the Alaskan and Pacific route, but indicating that he does not intend to oppose it. If he is at sea, where are the other ministers who share responsibility in this matter? For example, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources is reported to have said yesterday that, as he sees his duty it is to stimulate public discussion on these matters. One would have thought, Mr. Chairman, that his duty would be to develop policy instead of jumping around like a cat on a hot tin roof. We follow the minister all the way from Denver to his meeting the other day with representatives of the oil industry, and what do we find? We find the minister busily engaged in developing, not public opinion and certainly not informed public opinion, but simply in creating confusion in the minds of the Canadian people and, I am sure, in the minds of the American people as well.
Then we have the Minister of Communications getting into the act. The delightful climax is the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources suggesting to the Minister of Communications that others should think before they speak.
I am pointing this out at some length, Mr. Chairman, to remind everybody of the degree of confusion we have with the present size of the cabinet and the number of parliamentary assistants. We hear about all kinds of escalation these days. In view of the experience we have had, and in view of the proliferation of ministries and parliamentary assistants contemplated by this bill, I think it might be described as an escalation of confusion.
There are two results which are felt by the ordinary Member of Parliament, Mr. Chairman. There is increased
pressure on government members to conform to the party line and there is the degradation of the basic task of the parliamentarian which is to cast a critical and appraising eye on the executive power. It means more than ever that the only authentic Member of Parliament will be on the opposition side of the House if these measures carry. It shows the basic contempt with which the government views its own backbenchers, and it is another step in the direction of executive control of Parliament.
In short, Mr. Chairman, this clause of the bill constitutes an admission by the government of its own inability to pursue defined long term policies; it constitutes an admission of incompetence and a further attempt to substitute improvisation for planning and God knows, Sir, we have had enough improvisation. I say that it is no wonder the ordinary member on the other side of this House is unwilling to debate. I ask myself whether most of them are afraid to involve themselves because of the possible effect it might have on their future. It is no wonder that they want this debate to end quietly and soon. In general, their silence is an eloquent expression of their shame and I suppose that feeling does them some credit, but it is not enough. I say to them, through you, Sir, that if they believe in Parliament, if they believe in the control of government by Parliament, if they believe in themselves as parliamentarians, they should be raising their voices against this sham version of participatory democracy. By their silence, they are voicing their shame but at the same time they are displaying their servility.

Mr. Chairman, at this point of the debate on clause 14, which provides that the Governor in Council may by proclamation, establish a ministry of state, without going through the normal procedure, that is through legislation, I object once more to this manner of proceeding. Since the amendment I moved has been rejected, I wanted to intervene at this time to bring in new elements to this debate.
To replace my hon. colleagues in the context of this debate, I should like to set forth some basic principles that govern Canada. Canada is a sovereign country, although its charter is a foreign document. Our political system is a constitutional monarchy, in a federal system, in a parliamentary and democratic system, in a responsible government.
Mr. Chairman, the executive now consists of the Governor General, the Prime Minister and his cabinet. The Prime Minister is the major element.
The Governor General merely acts on behalf of the sovereign and on the advice of the cabinet. He summons, adjourns and dissolves parliament. He sanctions legislation and officiates at ceremonies. His main responsibility is to ensure the continuity of the state and to choose a Prime Minister in some rare and exceptional cases.
The members of the cabinet must normally be elected members from the party of the majority or from the party which obtained the confidence of the House.

April 2, 1971
Government Organization Act, 1970
Mr. Chairman, such is the spirit of the statutes which govern Canada. Therefore, it may be seen that the Governor in Council is nothing more than a ceremonial institution, and that it is not the Governor in Council who can establish "ministries of state", but rather the cabinet.
According to the British North America Act, parliament is composed of the Queen, the Senate and the House of Commons. The House of Commons remains the corner stone of the Canadian parliamentary system. Only the House may propose bills involving expenditure of monies or imposing new taxes.
Mr. Chairman, this is still the spirit of the legislation governing the Parliament of Canada. Well, clause 14 pushes aside parliament, which is still the supreme institution according to our statutes, to say that the cabinet itself will establish by proclamation and not by legislation the "ministries of state". The executive power is responsible to the elected representatives of the people for its actions and decisions. The House can overthrow the government by a non confidence vote, but the Prime Minister may at any time ask the Governor General to dissolve parliament and call a general election.
Therefore it means, Mr. Chairman, that according to the intent of the laws governing Canada, this House still remains a supreme institution. The government must answer to parliament for its decisions and administration.
But, in clause 14, the government gives itself an exceptional right not to proceed through parliament, concerning the establishment of "ministries of state". There is, in Canada, a genuine separation between the judicial and the political powers on which is based the principle of the independence of courts.
But parliament, Mr. Chairman, is still sovereign, under Canadian laws concerning the powers not dealt with under the BNA Act, including human rights.
Mr. Chairman, this shows again how the government, through clause 14, violates the laws which, since 1867, govern the administration of Canada. Parliament-and this is where things become most interesting if we consider the intent of the laws governing us-exercises control over the action of the executive power and can withdraw its confidence if necessary.
This means, Mr. Chairman, that it is not the government or the cabinet which gives parliament its power, but parliament which gives it to the government. It is an important factor of our parliamentary system and shows that if one wants to be logical, parliament should confer to the government the power to create those ministries of state and will in effect be creating them. It does not fall on the tool of parliament to create those ministries but on parliament itself.
Parliament must consider bills and the supremacy of the legislative power has never been challenged in Canada.
However, Mr. Chairman, the present government is challenging the supreme authority of that legislative institution, by introducing an exceptional legislation concerning the establishment of ministries.
I see that the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) is frowning, but I suggest to him that his department was indeed created by an act passed by the House of Commons while those ministries will not be established by an act of the House of Commons but rather by a proclamation of the governor in council.

Mr. Chairman, before lunch, I was demonstrating that clause 14 is in direct contradiction with the spirit and the letter of the legislation governing the land since 1867.
Parliament, always according to the spirit and the letter of the legislation governing Canada, exercises control over the actions of the executive power and can deny its confidence if need be. This has occurred in Canadian history. When you read the history of Canada, the mere fact that in some instances parliament denied its confidence in the government through a non-confidence motion or by overthrowing it proves to what extent the influence of parliament exceeds the executive power where decisions are concerned.
Parliament must study bills always according to the spirit of the law. The supremacy of the legislative power in this regard has never been questioned in Canada.
It is done nevertheless in the everyday political life. One quickly realizes that the balance of power now tends towards the executive on account of the great number of statutes. For instance, under the omnibus bill before us, we can no longer exercise complete control over all aspects of the legislative program submitted to parliament.
That is an extremely important point. The government made parliamentary reforms, they invented new ways of legislating in presenting, for instance, measures which we call omnibus bills and which include different parts often without any relation with one another. It is a kind of package deal that the House is asked to pass at top speed.
It does not take more time to pass a complex piece of legislation than a very simple one. Such a thing is inconceivable but it is done without hesitation under the guise of efficiency. Such is the system towards which parliament is moving progressively while losing little by little its control over the legislative power.
We can no longer thoroughly and objectively examine complex bills as we would a very simple measure. Bills from a member of the opposition have no chance of going through because the system is inadequate or because it is a bill the cabinet has decided not to approve.

April 2, 1971

The government has now decided to legislate through regulations without consulting the members and thus weaken the legislative power.
Now what is the object of clause 14 if not to legislate by creating "ministries of state" through a regulation or a royal proclamation instead of doing it by means of a debate and a vote in the House.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to give an explanation on a particular point. I do not object to the creation of ministries of state nor to the underlying principle, but I object to the form, to the procedure through which we are going to create ministries of state.
That will have the effect of increasing the power of the government to legislate by proclamation or regulations without consulting the House. It is that aspect of the question which prompts me to fight so desperately in the hope of bringing my colleagues, and particularly the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury), to revise their positions.
More and more, observers believe that the most important changes in the political institutions of Canada are no longer the result of the work of parliament, but rather of structures which properly speaking have no legislative power and which come directly under the jurisdiction of the executive power. For instance, the federal-provincial conferences as well as the different ministries of state which will be established.
Mr. Chairman, those ministries of state do not come under the jurisdiction of parliament, but under that of the executive power which will legislate more and more not through the democratic action of parliament but through its own authority, by way of royal proclamation or regulations.
Mr. Chairman, the rise of technocrats and the delegation of the responsibilities of the House to Crown corporations, to offices, to boards, to the cabinet itself, as it is done by Order in Council, have contributed and contribute more and more to a loss of prestige by parliament.
Mr. Chairman, more and more this government is legislating, controlling and influencing the Canadian policy not by using such a wonderful tool as parliament but on its own and through its own creatures, by establishing corporations not under the control of parliament, and by setting up, for example, regional information offices at the service of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) about which members of parliament are not allowed to say or know anything.
By proclamation, the government would give itself the power to create ministries of state, to appoint directly ministers of state at the head of these ministries, and this would therefore entail the expenditure of public funds which would escape control by parliament and we would get no information except, of course, the piece-meal information which the government agrees to give us.
Needless to say, Mr. Chairman, as members we are already in quite a precarious position in the eyes of the Canadian people as we cannot play the role we were given regardless which side of the House we are sitting,
Government Organization Act, 1970 namely of being informed and of transmitting this information to our ridings. We can no longer do this now because of the increasingly encroaching powers of the technocrats on members' actions.
This is basic. Several Liberal members behind the curtains are justified in complaining as do the Conservative the NDP and the Creditiste members, that the technocrats now have more importance and influence than the members, and this is nonsense.
The technocrats do not have to report to the people whereas the members do. In passing, let me say simply that each one of us regardless of his political views, will be responsible before our citizens at the next general election.
This means that if we are to account for our actions to the people we represent in parliament we are entitled to influence the policies and the administration.
Such are the spirit and the letter of the legislation governing our country. Mr. Chairman, when the executive, under the guise of efficiency, creates tools directly responsible to it and not to parliament, when the government arrogates the powers of parliament and delegates them to tools not responsible to the people, the prestige of parliament is being degraded, as well as the role of the member, whatever his political allegiance. We then prove inconsistent and indeed undemocratic.
We are all for efficiency and for "developing new policies" as prescribed by clause 14, since our present policy is antiquated and unintelligible. We wish the development of a new policy in various fields. We should like to know in which particular field these ministries will act, under whose authority and, precisely what responsibilities the ministers appointed to head them will assume. In addition, we should like to know whether these ministers will be responsible to parliament.
I ask myself the following question: will these ministers answer questions put by hon. members? In fact, the bill clearly says that the Governor in Council will appoint them. Therefore, if the minister heading the ministry condescends to reply, we shall get answer but, otherwise, they will do as does the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) concerning the CBC; they will provide no answer.
Mr. Chairman, this is why I fiercely oppose this clause that runs counter to the spirit and the letter of the legislation governing Canada since 1867.

That is an interesting suggestion, Mr. Chairman, particularly in light of what was put on the record on February 2 by the President of the Treasury Board. I point out that at the time of those changes, we hardly heard cries of dismay from members of the New Democratic Party. There were no alarms raised at that point. What were the powers that the Manitoba legislature, under that act, provided for the Lieutenant Governor in Council? I quote from the act:
Notwithstanding any act of the legislature the Lieutenant Governor in Council may determine the organization of executive government and of the various departments thereof, and for that purpose may
(a) establish, vary, or disestablish any department;
This is precisely the power that the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands was describing in these rather extravagant terms in respect of the present bill before the House. Under the Manitoba Executive Government Organization Act, the Lieutenant Governor in Council may also:
-determine or vary the duties and functions of any department and transfer any duties and functions from one department to another;
(c) determine or change the name of any department.
Now, Mr. Chairman, if what is happening here is so offensive to the traditions of Parliament, if what is happening is so inimical to the traditions of this Parliament, surely it is equally offensive and inimical to the traditions of the legislature of Manitoba. Where it appears to the Governor in Council that the requirements tor formulating and developing new and comprehensive policies in relation to any matter or matters coming within the responsibility of the Government of Canada warrant the establishment for the time being of a special portion of the public service of Canada presided over by a Minister charged with responsibility for the formulation and development of such policies, the Governor in Council may, by proclamation, establish a Ministry of State for that purpose.
If I may, I should like to mention something relating to my home province. If we are to be parochial in our thinking, let us at least talk about the environment from which we began our careers. When the Fathers of Confederation sat down together over 100 years ago, they did two things which now appear to be self-contradictory. If oil is discovered in commercial quantities off the coast of Nova Scotia, it will be seen that the positions of the Fathers of Confederation were contradictory indeed. The British North America Act provides that the boundaries of the province of Nova Scotia shall remain as they existed before confederation. If that is so, then the boundaries of Nova Scotia clearly extend to Sable Island, that spit of land cropping out in the Atlantic which has swallowed up so many ships and lives. Later, when defining the responsibilities of the Parliament of Canada, the
Government Organization Act, 1970 British North America Act, in a subsection of section 91, provides that the Parliament of Canada is to have exclusive jurisdiction over aids to navigation and the like. Sable Island is specifically mentioned. In my opinion, two parts of the British North America Act are contradictory. One part indicates that the province of Nova Scotia is to retain the jurisdiction it exercised over the territory that was Nova Scotia before the coming into effect of confederation, which brings in Sable Island.
The old maps show Sable Island. Nova Scotia, before confederation, had to provide navigation safeguards with respect to the island. But, another part of the British North America Act provides that the federal government or the Parliament of Canada shall have exclusive jurisdiction in certain areas. It mentions navigational safeguards, and specifically mentions Sable Island. I do not know how one can resolve this contradiction. I presume that the provisions of this subsection would not affect earlier sections of the British North America Act. Be that as it may, I submit that because Sable Island is specifically mentioned in the subsection I have just mentioned, the government could establish a ministry charged with responsibility for Sable Island, if I read clause 14 correctly.

Does the Prime Minister and his supergovernment really believe that the Canadian people are going to swallow one bitter pill after another, without ever calling him to account? The Prime Minister is custodian of the public purse, public welfare and Canadian institutions. There seems to be an assumption on the other side of the House that the Prime Minister can transcend all the rules of procedure and all the traditions which have been developed and nourished in the Canadian Parliament over the last 100 years. He is the sponsor of the bill before us, yet he has not been present at any of the debates in connection therewith.
There seems to be a misconception in the minds of those on the other side of the House as to just what is the role of the Prime Minister. There is surely some confusion as to whether or not the Prime Minister is even a mortal man. The Prime Minister does not own the public purse. He does not own the Canadian people. He does not own the institution of Parliament, all rumours to the contrary. The Prime Minister has confused his sacred trust with outright ownership. I go on record as informing him that he does not hold clear title to anything in Canada except his own personal property, like the rest of us. Parliament and the Canadian purse are the property of the Canadian people. The bill we are now debating makes the dangerous assumption that the Prime Minister is free to disburse funds at pleasure. It makes the assumption that the Prime Minister can dip into the public purse to reward obedience and servility on the part of his loyal subjects on the benches opposite. No Prime Minister in the history of Canada has ever

April 2, 1971

approached the august chair of chief minister with such total disregard for the responsibilities which are traditionally accepted and discharged by the holder of that high office.
All of us in this House know that the office of Prime Minister carries with it implied privileges which are not accorded to other parliamentarians. There are also responsibilities connected with that high office which do not have to be assumed or discharged by any other Canadian. Tabling legislation in this House in the sure knowledge that a clear majority of members supporting the government will ensure its passage is not a privilege; it is a responsibility. When a government holds a clear majority it is a public trust as well as a responsibility for the Prime Minister to ensure that the legislation tabled by him does not transcend the established limits of authority vested in him by the Canadian electorate.
Bill C-207 is a complete rejection of the responsibility assumed, presumably in good faith, by the Prime Minister. It constitutes a clear denial of the sacred trust vested in his high office; and I am prepared to challenge him to take this bill to the Canadian people by way of a referendum. If it is so important to him to have these super powers, let him get them directly from the people by their consent and I shall not complain. But he knows, as we know, Mr. Chairman, that the Canadian people would reject him and his preposterous demands out of hand. There is no justification for the powers the Prime Minister seeks in the bill before us. A Prime Minister who cannot govern with the largest cabinet in the history of this country is not likely to do any better simply by expanding it still further. Adding pomposity to the present Prime Minister's arrogance is not likely to get us better government.

Looking at the order paper, one would not get the impression that there has been a great deal of urgent public business prepared by the government for the consideration of this chamber. It is of interest to note that at second reading stage there are six items. The first is the Yukon Territory minerals bill, the second is the young offenders act, the third the Canada Labour (Standards) Code, the fourth the unemployment insurance legislation, fifth the weather modification bill, and sixth the Northwest Atlantic Fisheries Convention Act. Of those measures, I submit only three have any real substance and are of national importance-the young offenders bill and the two measures standing in the name of the Minister of Labour. In that connection I think even those measures would not take very much time of the House if the government were to indicate some willingness to remove the controversial and overburdening provisions contained in them.
After second reading we have two measures at the report stage. The first is legislation to provide for a grant for a heavy water plant in Nova Scotia. Then there is legislation dealing with weights and measures. On third reading we have the textile bill. So I do not see how the government can indicate it has a great, exciting program which has been held up by the discussion on this very important piece of legislation. In respect of part IV of the bill which is before us this afternoon, which is the proposal to create five new ministries of state, I would like to ask the government why we should consider increasing the size of this country's cabinet at this time.
Reference has been made to the size of the cabinet in the United Kingdom and the cabinet in the United States. I think it is of interest that in his state of the union address, the President of the United States proposed a reduction in the size of his cabinet. I should like to refer to an article by Lubor J. Zink in the Calgary Herald of February 19, 1971. The article states:
Paradoxically, Mr. Nixon says he can do with fewer cabinet ministers while Mr. Trudeau says he needs more.
Calling for a "sweeping reorganization of the executive branch" in his state of the union message last month, Mr. Nixon proposed to reduce the present 12 cabinet departments in Washington to eight.
We have 29. The reduction in the United States is a one-third reduction in the size of the cabinet. The article continues:
This, he said, we needed "if the government is to keep up with the times and with the needs of the people."
Mr. Nixon wants to retain unchanged four of the existing departments (state, treasury, defence and justice) which have clearly defined and indispensable roles, but seeks to consolidate the remaining eight into four which would be responsible for human resources, community development, natural resources, and economic development.
"Under this plan," Mr. Nixon said, "rather than dividing up our departments by narrow subjects, we would organize them around the great purposes of government. Rather than scatter-
Government Organization Act, 1970
ing responsibility by adding new levels of bureaucracy, we would focus and concentrate the responsibility for getting problems solved."
It's an imaginative and bold attempt to end the buck-passing paper-pushing practice among proliferating federal agencies which, Mr. Nixon said, have created "hopeless confusion for form and function."
No doubt the entrenched bureaucratic empires and their political protectors in Washington will fight Mr. Nixon's sweeping reorganization program tooth and nail.
I suggest that Bill C-207 interests the bureaucracy in this country because, after all, if there are to be up to five new ministries there will have to be supporting staffs. I think the comments of the editorialist in the Calgary Herald of February 18, 1971, are of interest here because a year or two ago we had a good program announced by the Prime Minister in which the public service was to be controlled and cut by 25,000 persons, as I recall the announcement of August, 1969. When all the smoke cleared we found that perhaps 300 people actually had been removed from the public service. In any event, that program has fallen by the wayside because now I believe there is a proposal to increase the public service by 8,000. I would quote from the editorial in this regard:
The great program to reduce the civil service in numbers is being replaced by a great new round of hiring. There is an allowance for hiring an additional 8,000 civil servants. This is one way to reduce unemployment, but it cannot be considered productive nor a realistic way of enlarging the nation's work force.
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, if there are to be new ministries there cannot help but be a larger supporting staff and I do not see any demonstrable need for such staff at this time. There certainly is no evidence that any member of the present administration is over-worked. We have a situation in which the Secretary of State I believe is now sojourning around southern France, and the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development is travelling around the South Pacific in a Boeing 707.
The ambitions of the Minister of Labour are a little less grandiose: he has gone to Montreal. I suppose he is working there in an effort to solve the transportation problem in this country. The locomotive engineers have been without a contract for ten months or more. This is a field of endeavour which is completely under the government's jurisdiction. If we have such an effective and hard working Minister of Labour, I wonder why in the past ten months he was not busy encouraging the parties to reach a contract instead of waiting for a strike to develop before doing anything and going where the action is.

The government has forgotten that we have a parliamentary system and think they are already operating under a presidential system. The roster system is another example of this. They forget their responsibilities to Parliament.
It is important to members of this House, perhaps more to some than to others, to remember that this parliamentary system is one of the bulwarks protecting the Canadian identity, and that if we further reduce parliamentary processes so as to implement presidential processes we will be reducing more and more our reasons for a separate Canadian identity. I think hon. members from the province of Quebec should be particularly conscious of this fact, because if we adopt presidential processes and make ourselves look more like the Americans, we will also, with the pressure of their presence already on this continent, tend to become part of the United States. If we look and act like them in everything we do, we may as well have their standard of living and become the real thing rather than a pale imitation. So I think it is very important that we stop going along this road toward a denial of the British parliamentary system for some sort of presidential system which would give us the worst of both systems.

speechtext:
that Bill C-36, relating to the control and management of the water resources of Canada, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works.
April 2, 1971

He said: Mr. Speaker, we have only an hour, so my remarks will not be long; and I am sure members on the government side will not filibuster this bill to the stage that we will not have a chance to vote on it. This bill was drafted and brought forward as a private member's public bill for the reasons set out in the explanatory note. As a member of this House with great interest and concern for the water resources of this country, it is my view that while government proposals were aimed in the right direction and contained some measure of remedial action against pollution and misuse of water resources, they did not go to the root of the issue. In my opinion, the federal government was not given the power it is entitled to exercise in a constitutional sense. The Fisheries Act, the Shipping Act, the Navigable Waters Protection Act and other measures have been on the statute books for a great many years. If this legislation had been used it would probably have been sufficient to prevent a great many of the problems which we and the next generation will have to face.
The official aspect of the problem has been apparent to a great many people in the northern part of Canada, and for that reason this bill was presented to the House. The Navigable Waters Protection Act has been in force for a great many years, since well into the last century. The act contains provisions and sanctions which specifically prohibit certain action with regard to the use of navigable waters. For many years prior to the time it was discovered by Sir Alexander Mackenzie, and for many years piior to that by the native people, the Peace River has been one of the important, main arteries of navigation in northern Canada. Some years ago the province of British Columbia was permitted to erect a very substantial dam on the river, known as the Bennett dam. I have never rejected the need for the proper development and use of water resources in the north for the production of power, Mr. Speaker, but I think it must be done under rules and regulations which take into account what is best for the nation as a whole. This was not the case with this particular dam.
The federal government of the day, a Liberal government, failed to insist upon the province of British Columbia and the hydro agency which was acting as a Crown agency for the government, filing an application under the Navigable Waters Protection Act, filing the plan and a statement of its requirements indicating the amount of water to be impounded by the construction of the dam. The federal government and the provincial government of Alberta of that day failed to consider the possibility that the erection of the dam would cause to those agrarian dwellers below the area where it was constructed, a substantial amount of damage. Construction was allowed to proceed and no attempt was made to compei the province of British Columbia to comply with the Navigable Waters Protection Act
At the time I asked a number of questions. I pressed the government and the then Minister of Public Works who held responsibility for enforcement of the act. I pressed the Minister of Justice, who said that the works being constructed by the agency of the province of British Columbia were works to which the act applied. I
Water Resources Management Act pressed the Minister of Public Works to know whether the government of Canada was proceeding to require the province of British Columbia to file a plan and make application to the department in order to secure permission to proceed under the act. They did not do this, the dam was built and as a result the prophecy of myself and others came to pass. The drainage levels of the river have been diminished. This has happened with the Athabasca delta as well, and it has affected the level in the Mackenzie River navigation system. The result may be permanent damage to future transportation in that area. At the present time we do not know what ill effects it will have.
I could deal with this matter at length, Mr. Speaker, but I know that other hon. members wish to speak and are anxious that this bill receive second reading today. It was for these reasons and because a number of other acts are along the same lines that I introduced this bill. According to the explanatory note, it vests in the federal government the full measure of power which I believe the federal government has to exercise in order to deal with the problems of misuse and pollution of water resources. This is a problem on which we must legislate in the interests of those who come after us, Mr. Speaker. It is not enough for us to legislate for it today; we must legislate for 100 or 200 years hence. The present legislation, while aimed in the right direction, is not adequate and does not go far enough.
I am not suggesting that there is not a role for the provincial government. There is, and there must be, an overriding authority-but that can only be in the federal government. I think it should go a great distance under the existing Constitution. However, if it is found that the existing Constitution does not permit the federal government to go as far as it should in laying down guidelines, then it is for us to alarm the people of Canada so that they will demand that the final and overriding authority be vested in the federal government.
With these remarks, Mr. Speaker, I shall resume my seat. I hope that other hon. members will have the opportunity to make contributions before second reading is given to the bill before five o'clock.

subtopic: WATER RESOURCES MANAGEMENT ACT

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my purpose in rising to speak on Bill C-36 is to outline the current status of the Peace-Athabasca delta project and show that the federal government is co-ordinating with the provinces and is taking action on that very severe problem. In doing so, it may be helpful if I reviewed very briefly the problem in the delta and the establishment of the federal-provincial task force. I should like to summarize particularly our co-operative project with the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia. I shall outline and summarize the objective and design of the delta project and the work presently under way.
Hon. members are aware that low water levels have occurred in the delta for several years. This has resulted
April 2, 1971

Water Resources Management Act in ecological change to the natural habitat tor fish and wildlife, with consequent damage to their populations. The contributing factors to the low water level are low precipitation in the Peace and Athabasca river basins and the regulation of the Peace River by the construction of the Bennett dam.
As hon. members may remember, in early January of this year ministerial agreement was reached between the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry (Mr. Davis) for the government of Canada and Hon. J. D. Henderson, for the province of Alberta, to establish a joint task force which would be responsible for investigating the delta problem. Subsequently, the government of Saskatchewan agreed to participate in the study, and the government of British Columbia to provide technical information on its Peace River regulation. Because the problem lies largely within a national park, involves an interprovincial river and has adversely affected the livelihood of the local Indian population, the federal government has taken the lead in initiating and funding this investigation. Treasury Board has given its approval to the project, its cost and timing. We have hired a competent consultant, Mr. D. M. Hornby of Calgary, as project director. Mr. Hornby has been on the job now since mid-January, operating with a small professional staff out of the Peace-Athabasca delta project office in Edmonton.
The key element in mounting a co-operative intergovernmental effort is effective organization. In this case the task force consists of an intergovernmental liaison team, a technical committee and the project director and his staff. The intergovernmental liaison team has a member from Canada, Alberta and Saskatchewan. The chairman of the liaison is Mr. F. J. Forbes, head of the prairie regional section, planning division, water operation and planning branch, Department of Fisheries and Forestry. The team's function is to provide liaison on questions of policy and administrative matters between the project director and the governments involved.
The technical committee consists of senior personnel from federal and provincial agencies who are responsible for resources management in the Peace-Athabasca delta area. This committee provides technical advice to the project director. Co-operation, a point stressed in the hon. member's bill, among the members of the task force has been excellent. To date the intergovernmental liaison team has met three times and the technical committee has met twice, including a field trip to the delta on March 24, 1971, which was just last week.
The joint federal-provincial technical committee recommended that a staged approach be adopted. The first stage would focus on restoring water levels in the delta by the spring of 1972. The objective for the first stage as drafted for the technical committee is as follows:
Within the Peace-Athabasca delta and Lake Athabasca area to assess, by September 1, 1971, the environmental effects of the future hydrologic regime (with Shrum generating station, Bennett Dam In operation) on the following:
(1)	Vegetation pattern
(2)	Fish production
(3)	Wildlife habitat
(4)	Navigation, and
the consequent influence on the socio-economic status of residents, and to recommend what immediate or long-range action, if any, should be taken.
I must stress, Mr. Speaker, that the project is focusing on the immediate problem of restoring water levels by the spring of 1972. Ecologists feel that this is a critical period and that low water levels beyond that time could result in permanent ecological damage in the delta. At the same time, the technical committee recognizes that there are broader environmental issues and long-range implications involved and may recommend additional studies to consider them.
The total estimated cost for the first stage of the project is close to $1 million. Expenditures have been budgeted over a 12-month period ending in March, 1972. The bulk of the expenditure will occur this summer. Expenditure in 1972 will cover the completion of reports and preparation of recommendations for future work. The thrust of the investigations will be ecology, at an estimated cost of $227,000, and hydrology at an estimated cost of $158,000. As noted earlier, the federal government will bear the bulk of the expenditures. Ministerial discussions are under way with Alberta to obtain technical assistance on the project. Also, the intergovernmental liaison team is reviewing the legal aspects of the delta problem.
Having described the Peace-Athabasca delta project, Mr. Speaker, I want to summarize the key developments. First, a project office has been established in Edmonton. The following professional staff for the office has been seconded: a planner from the Department of Fisheries and Forestry, a hydrologist from the water resources division, Alberta Department of Agriculture, and an ecologist from the Canada Wildlife Service; second, a field camp with a capacity for 25 men has been established at Fort Chipewyan; third, a contract was let in early March for an ice-thickness and water-depth survey in the delta. It is a part of the ecological investigations. This work, it is hoped, will be completed shortly. Fourth, contract proposals have been invited for a socio-economic study of the importance of the resources of the area; and fifth, office work is under way on the hydrologic and ecological investigations.
In regard to the purpose of our deliberations this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, which is mainly to assess the need for additional legislation on water resource management, the Peace-Athabasca delta project provides two important conclusions: first, the government in co-operation with the provinces is taking positive action to correct the delta problem; second, the project is evidence that a major intergovernmental effort involving several governments can be mounted quickly under existing legislation. The question then is, what need have we for Bill C-36?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry (Mr. Corbin) has given the members of the House an outline of what is now taking place under the auspices of the task force to which he referred which is

April 2, 1971

to deal with ecological and other problems created in the Peace River-Athabasca delta area. Without decrying or downgrading the work which he outlined, I suggest that if ever there was a classic case of locking the barn door after the horse was stolen, this is it. Certainly I would not agree with the conclusion he enunciated in his last sentence, that the proposal contained in the bill introduced by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) is unnecessary. Nothing is further from the truth. Perhaps it is all the more necessary in light of the experience of the disastrous or near-disastrous results that have become apparent from the construction of the Portage Mountain dam on the Peace River in the province of British Columbia.
As the hon. member for Peace River has said, this whole question has become one of increasing and urgent importance. The drafting of the bill is rather novel in some respects. I do not intend to go into the details of its merits, but there is one point which strikes me as being the key point if I understand his intent correctly. He is suggesting the obvious, that in any river or river basin which is interprovincial, in light of the current situation in this country we have a situation where the constitutional jurisdiction with respect to something being done for the general advantage of Canada must be recognized and brought into play. If this is what the hon. member for Peace River is seeking to do with this bill, then the principle should certainly commend itself to this House.
The story of the development of the Portage Mountain dam, which has been christened the Bennett dam in honour of the Premier of my province, has gone on for years. Some of the key decisions in relation to it were made during the period I was not a member of this House, between 1958 and 1962. I therefore did not have the opportunity to express myself on the subject in this forum. During the period when the basic decisions were being made, the government of the province of Alberta appeared to remain silent and uninterested in what was going on across the western provincial boundary. It should have been obvious to anyone with any knowledge what would happen because of the impact of building that dam to hold back the normal flow of the Peace River. It would not only affect the river within the province of British Columbia but the portion which lies in the province of Alberta and, indeed, the entire Mackenzie River drainage system which, of course, involves the Northwest Territories.
The federal government has jurisdiction over the Northwest Territories. I have always been amazed that definitive, joint action was not taken at that time by the government of Alberta and the federal government to make it clear to Mr. Bennett that in the national interest he must be called upon to recognize that something was involved which went far beyond the boundaries of one province and, therefore, directly or indirectly affected all the people of Canada.
I have a bill on the order paper which is not unrelated to the subject matter of Bill C-36. My bill is C-105, to amend the Navigable Waters Protection Act. By the simple addition of one section to that act, it will state
Water Resources Management Act
"This act is binding on Her Majesty in right of Canada or a province or any agent thereof." Hon. members may recall that an amendment in these terms was agreed to last year when dealing with the amendments to the Fisheries Act. I proposed an amendment to the amending bill at the report stage.
As far as I know, this particular formula was first incorporated into a piece of legislation in the International River improvements Act of 1955. This is made clear in the explanatory note of my bill which states that many activities of governments, either at the federal or provincial level, and more particularly their agents in the form of Crown corporations such as hydro authorities, impinge on the economy, ecology and whole pattern of development in the country, in much the same way as activities of large private corporations.
This has been one of the uncertainties about the question of whether the province of British Columbia was in fact required to secure a permit other than under the Navigable Waters Protection Act for the construction of that dam. It was in effect being built by the province through its agent the Crown corporation, the B.C. hydro power authority. This is one of the ambiguities this House should take steps to clarify at the earliest possible date. It would be a useful step in augmenting the purpose which the hon. member for Peace River seeks in his bill.
The issue raised by Bill C-36 is highlighted by the fact that a provincial waters act has just been introduced for first reading in the legislature of the province of British Columbia. According to the reports I have received, the minister introducing the bill, Hon. Ray Wil-liston, said it was his intent to introduce this bill for first reading in the current session of the legislature. He said it would be open for consideration and broad discussion. As a result of that, he said it was his intention to introduce an identical or similar bill at the next session of the provincial legislature.
The most significant part of the statement by that minister was that a jurisdictional vacuum exists with regard to water resources, their use, control and management. Because of this he felt that the legislature should move to fill that vacuum before some other authority sought to take it over. I am not privy to all that may have gone on in the considerations of the Lieutenant Governor in Council prior to the introduction of that bill.
I mention it to underline the importance of the subject matter raised today by the hon. member for Peace River. In the previous session there was extensive discussion in the House and in the standing committee with regard to a federal act in respect of our waters. Apart from any other implications, it muddied the waters in the matter of constitutional jurisdiction over our national water resources.
I am happy, therefore, to support the principle of the bill introduced by the hon. member for Peace River although its terminology appears to be unusual, for which reason I cannot say whether I would agree with

April 2, 1971
Water Resources Management Act every particular. However, the idea behind it is one which I feel the House should support, and I for one would like to see the measure referred for consideration to a standing committee of the House. I am sure there are few things which are more important or more urgent today than making wise use from now on of our natural water resources.
Apart from what happened in connection with the Columbia River under the agreement entered into with the United States, what has occurred on the Peace River, Athabasca and Mackenzie river systems as a result of the construction of the dam at Portage Mountain just west of the British Columbia-Alberta boundary is a classic example of the unwise use of our resources. I hope the House will seriously consider allowing this bill to be read the second time so that it can be considered in more detail by the appropriate standing committee.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to rise and make a few observations about this bill. I should say at the outset that I support it, believing that such legislation is a necessity at the present time. The need is well illustrated by the downstream effects of the W.A.C. Bennett dam.
What has taken place in the Peace-Athabasca delta has been widely discussed in the last year or so, particularly with reference to the damage to the ecology which has resulted from an insufficient flow of water down the Peace River since the dam was completed. I have had an opportunity to review the Hansards of the early sixties when this dam was being planned and during the early phases of its construction, and I have found-as my hon. friend from Peace River (Mr, Baldwin) has pointed out-[DOT] that the question of whether the government of British Columbia had applied to the federal government under the terms of the Navigable Waters Protection Act was raised on many occasions in the House of Commons. But for reasons which are unknown to me, the federal Liberal government of the day chose to ignore those questions.
This is a good example of the kind of thing we had in mind when talking about another bill earlier today. In the Liberal cabinet of that day, quantity was not lacking but the quality of the ministers was not necessarily commensurate. If the ministers responsible at that time had really been equal to their jobs, the situation we face today might have been avoided.
There is another lesson to be learned from this. On many occasions the Liberal government in power at the time, like the one which is in power today, blindly opposed any suggestions from the opposition no matter how good or beneficial they might have been, simply because they came from the opposition. I hope the present government and hon. members who are sitting opposite me now and smiling will bear this in mind and do what they can to see that such obvious mistakes are not repeated.
What happened with regard to the construction of the Bennett dam and the destruction which occurred downstream is an example not only of negligence on the part of the governments of the day, that is, the federal government and the government of British Columbia, but also of the manner in which huge interests are able to run roughshod over the desires of ordinary citizens. It also shows that governments ought not to be rushed into proceeding with projects of this kind as soon as they are conceived. This has particular relevance today to the proposal to construct a Mackenzie Valley oil pipeline. It is evident that the government is overly anxious to proceed with this project, though it may well be that research in connection with such schemes has not yet reached the point at which we could ensure that the ecology of the area and the interests of the people who live there would not be adversely affected.
I was interested to hear the comments made by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry (Mr. Corbin). He told us that a federal-provincial task force had been set up and described what it would be doing. It appears that one of the most important parts of the necessary studies has been omitted, that is, the effect of the decreased water level of the Peace River on the town of Peace River itself. As is well known, the town has launched a lawsuit against B.C. Hydro for damages done to its water intake system. The town has had to spend considerable amounts of money to reconstruct its water intake system in the river, and so far it has been unable to obtain any sort of compensation for this extra expenditure. The government should give serious consideration to extending its study to include the difficulty which has occurred in the operation of the water intake system owned by the town of Peace River.
I was also pleased to learn that a technical committee and field commission have been set up at Fort Chipe-wyan to study conditions in the Athabasca delta. It is important that we assess the extent of the damage done in the area. It is also important we should determine whether or not this damage is reversible and determine, also, what might be done to repair the damage which exists. I have received communications from the Indian people in the area, their chiefs and their advisers-people who live very close to nature and who probably understand it better than most of our ecologists. They are pointing out the advantages of dams of the type beavers build which would raise the water to the level desired while not impeding the overflow experienced when the water rises in the spring.
The vegetation changes in the area have become obvious. What used to be a wide, swampy area covered by water during part of the year is now grown over with tall grasses and acres of tall red willows. The fall in the water level has greatly impaired the ability of the native people to make a living by trapping. The parliamentary secretary told us that socio-economic studies would be undertaken, but if I remember correctly there was no indication that the committee would include a particular person charged with carrying out such studies.
I think it is fair to say that the chief source of income for the people in the region of Fort Chipewyan, or one of the chief sources, is trapping, particularly muskrat,

April 2, 1971

though other fur-bearing animals also. Fishing has also been adversely affected; there is no question of that. This can be substantiated by the fact that welfare costs in the region have gone up by leaps and bounds in the last couple of years. I would close by indicating that in view of the fact that making a living has become more difficult, the incomes of the people in the area of the Peace-Athabasca delta have been substantially reduced. As a result, we must consider what alternatives we can offer these people.
In this regard we must seriously ask ourselves, who is the fellow who caused the problem in the first place, and see what can be done to hold him responsible at least in part. As I said before, the fellow who is responsible is in fact a group of fellows: the federal government, which failed to look at the situation to begin with; the British Columbia government, which in its rush to construct this hydro project did not give due consideration to the effects it would have on neighbouring communities; and the Alberta government, which was either sleeping at the switch or for some reason or other did not look at the situation at all while the project was being developed.
In conclusion, I think this is a good bill. I do not want to see it talked out and I hope it passes, to the benefit of all Canadians.

Just to round out this particular point before getting back to the subject of the bill, I would say that when hon. members opposite stop making inaccurate statements about us, I will stop telling the truth about them.
Bill C-36 in many ways catches the spirit of government legislation which has already been passed. Its explanatory note states in part:
The purpose of this bill is to concentrate and use the full powers of the federal government to control and manage the sea and fresh water resources of Canada in the public interest; and the provision, where necessary, for co-operation with the provinces to this end.
Compare this statement with the first paragraph of the explanatory note to Bill C-144, the Canada Water Act, which was proclaimed law on September 30, 1970. It read as follows:
Bill C-144, an act to provide for the management of the water resources of Canada including research and the planning of programs relating to the conservation and development of water resources.
There is obvious duplication between that bill and Bill C-36. I should like to examine the Canada Water Act a little more closely, but before doing so I would point out that if my memory serves me correctly we had members of the opposition sitting on the National Resources and Public Works Committee during those 34 meetings on the Canada Water Act, to which I referred, who were very vocal in regard to protecting provincial rights. The suggestion being made in this bill, that the federal government should be taking a stronger stand as far as jurisdiction over water resources in Canada is concerned, conflicts with the previous stand taken by some hon. members opposite.
From a personal point of view I very much sympathize with the House leader of the opposition. I am one who feels that the federal government should have stronger constitutional powers in regard to handling many phases of resource development in this country, one of these being water development. For this reason I am a very strong advocate of the greater use of the elastic clause in the Canadian Constitution.
The Canada Water Act had its origins in two major national meetings, the Resources for Tomorrow conference in 1961 and the pollution conference of 1966. It was conceived in 1967 and drafted mainly in the spring and summer of 1969 under the auspices of the present government. Its concepts were presented to the Canadian public in a policy paper in late August, 1969, and was formally introduced to the House of Commons on November 5 of the same year. After many days of debate in both the House of Commons and the Senate, and
