Water Resources Management Act
nearly 40 public hearings, it was passed by Parliament on June 26, 1970.
Surely, throughout all this period there was plenty of communication and opportunity for communication. I often feel that communication is one of the cheapest things we have to offer in this world, yet sometimes it is one thing of which least use is made. If we could at all levels of government achieve complete co-operation instead of participating in bickering matches, then in such an atmosphere of harmony we would be able to do far more for the country.
Why did the federal government pass such legislation? First, because it was obvious to the majority of political leaders, to academics and industrialists, to government officials and to the public generally that the pattern of water resource development and utilization across Canada was not fully satisfactory despite some excellent programs in certain areas and on certain topics. Secondly, with the federal government having certain responsibilities in the field of water resources and the provincial governments other responsibilities, a framework for a co-operative program was needed.
In the event that the province should not act and that there is not federal-provincial co-operation in bringing in a constructive program for the proper utilization of water resources, in the final analysis the Canada Water Act suggests that the federal government should act unilaterally. This comment was placed on the record on a couple of occasions by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene), the gentleman who still holds that portfolio today. Here is where the elastic clause in the Canadian Constitution would come into play.
We may run into situations in the future concerning the disposition of certain provincial arguments about matters which could involve the subject under discussion today. It is quite possible that this aspect of the Canada Water Act will end up in the Supreme Court of Canada. But surely this is how the laws of a nation are solidified and put on the books once and for all so that they may be changed only by further acts of Parliament as times and as needs require. I think we should be prepared to take our chances in this regard in respect of any act which goes through this Parliament. I think the time is ripe in Canada, if we do not get stronger amendments to the Canadian Constitution, for the elastic clause to be exercised and questioned in the Supreme Court on such issues as this. We cannot continue forever having long hassles over the resources of this country, involving long discussions between federal and provincial governments at a time when immediate action and immediate decision is an absolute necessity.
Unfortunately, the inadequacies of Canadian water resources' development and utilization were abundantly clear. Under these circumstances, the federal government felt it had to equip itself with the legislative authority to meet fully its responsibilities to remedy these deficiencies.
Recognizing on the one hand the divided jurisdiction in water matters and, on the other hand, the very real gains in efficiency and effectiveness by a comprehensive multipurpose approach to water development and utilization, the federal government set out to build a legislative platform for joint federal-provincial undertakings and in the final analysis for unilateral action by the federal government if necessary, but only as a last resort. To this end, the Canada Water Act contains six principal parts. In these six principal parts I think hon. members of this House will recognize that the bill before us in private members' hour, Bill C-36, in fact in some respects overlaps the Canada Water Act.
The first of the six points is consultation-joint examination of problems to reach accord on certain areas and subjects requiring joint action and those most appropriately undertaken by each government alone. The second point involves comprehensive water management-joint comprehensive planning of river or lake basins, regions or coastal strips and joint implementation of those plans. Perhaps there is a very strong case here that the Peace River should be under a river basin plan. The third point is water quality management-joint designation of water quality areas, formation or designation of a management agency, water quality planning, implementation of those plans, a prohibition against the deposit of wastes except as prescribed by the regulations, and the assessment of fees and charges.
The fourth point involves nutrient control-a prohibition against the import or manufacture in Canada of cleansing agents or water conditioners containing more than the prescribed content of nutrients. The fifth point deals with inspection and enforcement-provision for inspectors to examine effluents, cleansing agents and water conditioners; fines for contravention of the prohibitions, plus the power to close the offending plants if necessary.
The sixth point is public information-a program to inform the public of the state of water resource development in Canada, to increase the understanding by the public of the problems of environmental degradation, and to use public leaders in an advisory capacity. These are the key features of the Canada Water Act. How do they work or how is it intended they will work? One of the major considerations certainly is consultation. In summing up I would say that from this examination of current federal legislation one finds that the subject matter of Bill C-36 is largely redundant. Measures to preserve and enhance environmental quality are included in recent federal legislation and, in addition, the government has before the House Bill C-207 which has even further implications for anti-pollution legislation.
